Thank you, Ambassador. I'm honored to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. The group is encouraged by the forward-looking section on science, technology and innovation. We believe that the advent of digital technologies, including in finance over the past decade, has represented the greatest progress and accelerant for development for developing countries, facilitating greater financial inclusion, achieving the SDGs, more innovative fiscal strategies, and enabling greater incentives for private investments. We believe that FFD4 is an opportunity for us to double down on progress made so far and raise the ambition for SDI, which we note that both developing and developed countries have collectively agreed to. We are therefore encouraged by the references in the zero draft to enhancing coordination in SDI development and policy at the national and international levels. The need to develop Digital public infrastructure and enabling domestic environments for SDI provides a good foundation for further discussion. We are also pleased to see that the group's earlier suggestions on anti competition regulation have been addressed. While this is a good basis, we believe that this section can benefit from greater specificity in its recommendations, particularly on capacity building support for developing countries and to reflect more positive examples of successful uses of financial technologies and financial products for development. In this regard, the group would like to make the following points. While we agree that coordination at the national and international levels is important, we would like to see more details on coordination between the technology and other relevant sectors and between public and private actors to steer technological change towards addressing pressing development challenges. We also appreciate the calls for references to capacity building for developing countries. However, it is unclear at this stage what this would entail. For example, the group had previously suggested into earlier language on developing the digital competencies of public officials and institutions of developing countries. We would like to see this included. We would also like to see stronger language on the need for STI regimes to be better aligned with the SDGs and national development goals. We would also like to see the section delve into the impact of STI development on labor. We would like to see references to actions to one, mitigate how rapid technological change can result in brain drain in developing countries, how it can guide technological development to be labor complementary rather than labor replacing, directing resources to education and training, especially to promote workforce upskilling and reskilling. We would also like to see references to deepening public private partnerships for the express purpose of the following, One, encouraging entrepreneurship, which we note is not mentioned in this section and only twice throughout the entire document. Two, developing local innovation ecosystems and ensuring that innovation in developing countries can reach global markets. And three, supporting policies towards open science and open innovation and the co-development of technologies. Lastly, the group reiterates our call for a multilateral fund to stimulate innovation and cooperation, facilitate shared global research, technology transfer, and best practices, such as through joint innovation challenges, and to enable developing countries to benefit from new and emerging technologies. Connectivity is essential to adopt high tech in these sectors of society so that they can be included in this digital development in spheres such as education, health, and the economy. Nevertheless, we should also bear in mind the risks posed by these issues. And in this sense, we would like to offer for the consideration of the co-facilitators the possible incorporation of the fight against cybercrime as an essential pillar in order to ensure digital security and inclusion in all countries. The growing digitalization of our economy and of public services has created unprecedented opportunities for development, there is no doubt about that, but it has also exposed states and citizens to risks such as financial fraud, data theft, and also attacks against critical infrastructures. This is why we would encourage to include in the final document commitments to strengthen national capacities as well as international cooperation when it comes to cybersecurity, thus ensuring that our digital transformation is safe, accessible, and equitable for all. There is an urgent need to address the digital divide and digital cooperation at a time when the need for equal access to these technologies has become more evident than ever. Therefore, we are pleased to see that this chapter rightly acknowledges the persisting inequality in innovation and technology access and that developing countries face challenges in leveraging the potential of STI, further impeding their sustainable development. The Holy See has consistently advocated for inclusive, responsible and secure digital cooperation and connectivity. With this in mind, we believe that the text can be improved in some areas. We believe that this chapter would benefit from stronger language on the need for investment in the critical infrastructure that locks many developing countries, including countries in special situations, out of harnessing the benefits of STI. We welcome paragraph 58 and 59. We note that technological advances are beneficial but must also be managed to avoid unintended consequences, such as those mentioned here which cause environmental degradation or worsen gender inequality. On paragraph 59a, we would like to see language which recognises that data is both a product of and an enabler for science, technology and innovation. On 59c, we would like to see clarity from the COFAX on what is meant by TRIPS flexibilities so we can clarify how they would be used to contribute to innovation and also to understand what's missing from existing agreements. We believe that in addition to ensuring access to financial services to promote financial inclusion, we also need to equip individuals with the necessary knowledge to utilize financial and digital advancement for their financial health. Enhancing financial and digital literacy will empower individuals to make informed financial decisions, safeguard financial health, and contribute meaningfully to economic development. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Indonesia. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil, to be followed by Zimbabwe and ITU. Now, Brazil, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. I'd like to start by saying there's a very clear link between science and technology and development. When we look at the research by Cesar Hidalgo and Ricardo Hausmann and their work on economic complexity, we will realize that they used big data models to confirm things that development economists have been saying since the '50s and '60s. So industrialization, economic diversification, the production and export of high value-added and technology-intensive goods will ultimately determine the economic growth patterns and the well-being of populations and nations in the long term. So the commodity trap is still very, very relevant and we can address this through science and technology. What was also pointed out by development economists of the past is that the international technological diffusion is very unequal and puts developing countries in an unfavorable situation. We hear a lot of, let's say, lip service to technological transfers, for the lack of a better word, with the usual caveat in our text. With regards to the text, in para 56 we'd like to add innovation and technology production and access. Further down, environmental degradation and worsen gender and racial inequality. Thank you, Chair. Technology is a key lever for achieving the sustainable development goals. However, achieving this goal requires mobilizing significant investments. In this regard, we propose the following recommendations. In paragraph 59B, stable and adequate regulatory frameworks are key to digital development. We recommend explicitly mention the need for strengthened regulatory frameworks alongside competition laws. Additionally, we call for enhanced international cooperation between national regulatory bodies and competition authorities. In paragraph 59F, to ensure equitable access to AI, adequate financing should also cover AI enabling infrastructure. In paragraph 59G, digital infrastructure should be explicitly recognized as an area for enhanced national and international cooperation. Additionally, when referencing to actors in the STI system, we recommend mentioning relevant organizations such as the ITU to foster greater collaboration between multilateral development banks and the UN system. Regarding paragraph 60, We acknowledge the recognition that the lack of digital infrastructure remains a significant barrier for many developing countries, however, we see a need for a clearer distinction between digital infrastructure and digital public infrastructure, as well as for a stronger call to, for multi-stakeholder collaboration to mobilize investment in digital infrastructure. In this regard, we recommend expanding the commitment in paragraph 68 to explicitly include financing gaps and coordinate investment in digital infrastructure alongside digital public infrastructure. We also suggest adding a subparagraph calling for increased collaboration among governments, development finance institutions, the private sector, and the UN system to share knowledge, develop financing instruments, and jointly mobilize resources. This collaboration should accelerate investments in resilient and inclusive digital infrastructure, building on and complementing existing initiatives such as the Digital Infrastructure Investment Initiative. Thank you.
I thank the representative of ITU. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Djibouti, to be followed by OMEC Mexico and Latin DAD.

Thank you, facilitator. My delegation at the outset on the self-estimate made by respectively on behalf of the United States of China and the LDCs. We make these comments in our national capacity. The use of less polluting energy-efficient technologies for the environment as well. And lastly, science, technology, and innovation can stimulate the transformation of our economies by fostering the creation of new jobs, services and innovative services for our modern societies. We also propose adding in this section a mention to South-South cooperation when it comes to STI. Uh, thank you, Chair, uh, Steam Co-Chair, distinguished delegates, and honored participants. I'm Artemisa Montilman from OMEC, speaking on behalf of Latin DAD and the CSFD mechanism. It's a privilege to address this team gathering as we come together in pursuit of shared progress and global cooperation. We consider this section will be strengthened by a more explicit recognition of the importance of inclusive and transparent governance in science, technology and innovation. While the focus on harnessing the data and AI revolution is valuable, a more holistic and coordinated approach will be better support, will better support the twin digital and climate transitions. To ensure truly inclusive and sustainable progress, it is essential to integrate mechanism that promote transparency, equity and broad based participation in decision making. Member states have a unique opportunity to reinforce global cooperation by establishing an intergovernmental, inclusive, and participatory mechanism at the UN to evaluate new and emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, and the societal, economic, environmental, and climate-related impacts. Ensuring meaningful engagement at all levels along multi-stakeholders participation will contribute to a governance framework that is both accountable and responsive. Additionally, there is growing recognition of the importance of public oversight and balanced regulatory measures to ensure that innovation serves common good while fostering sustainable and equitable development. A more inclusive approach to financing for development will also be instrumental in ensuring that benefits of SDI are widely shared. The digital and technological divide continues to pose challenges, disproportionately affecting women, girls, people with disabilities, and marginalized communities in developing nations. Many countries face obstacles related to resources, infrastructure, and investment, which limit their ability to fully participate in the global innovation economy. Strengthening financial commitments to women, girls, led innovation and entrepreneurship while expanding access to digital tools, STEM education, and research funding will help bridge this gap and unlock new opportunities for all. Technology transfers from developed to developing countries plays a crucial role in fostering inclusive innovation. Many transformative scientific advancements remain concentrated in wealthier nations, contributing to persistent global inequalities. Prioritizing equitable partnerships that facilitates access to patents, open source technological solutions, and tailored capacity building programs can empower developing countries to adapt and implement innovation suited to their specific needs. Despite their immense contributions, women and girls remain underrepresented in scientific research, innovation, and entrepreneurship. Expanding development financing for women and girls in STEM research and technology enterprises while integrating gender impact assessments into funding decisions will help ensure that financial activity promotes inclusive economic growth that unintentionally reinforcing disparities. We would like to reaffirm the importance of ensuring that decision-making processes within the UN uphold the principles of democratic participation, transparency, and civic accountability. An open, inclusive, and consultative approach to global economic governance will strengthen trust and foster more effective collaboration. We will submit specific suggestions for paragraphs in the written statement. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Ambassador. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. On the data monitoring and follow-up section of this document, the group agrees that strengthened data monitoring and follow-up mechanisms are vital for us to diagnose gaps and ensure sustained progress on FFD. It is our view that the section on data should be considered a cross-cutting issue and not relegated as an afterthought to the end of the document. We should be extolling the virtue and necessity of strong and robust data in all sections of this document, recognizing that good and accurate data can enable developing countries to properly diagnose financing gaps and address the consequent challenges accordingly. In this section, it is important we think that we call for strengthened data and statistical capacities for developing countries. We would like to reiterate the following points: one, we are encouraged by the calls for more disaggregated data and statistics, and we would like to see this retained; 2... We also welcome the strong reference to SDG indicator 17.3.1 as a baseline for our monitoring of the financing of, of, of financing data, which we believe provides further statistical cla- clarity to developing countries on the support received. We would also like to see a call for innovative data collection methodologies, technologies and sources for developing policy relevant information, which provide opportunities to generate real time information and complement official statistics. We also note the calls for increased coordination on data and also like to specify that there should be strengthened investment in and collaboration with national and international statistical agencies, including through public-private partnerships. We also call for the document to acknowledge voluntary non-financial and sustainability data reported by the private sector, which we believe we should also tap on where appropriate to encourage robust data on private enterprises' impact on development while reducing fragmentation and reporting burdens, taking into account national circumstances and contexts. We also call for the multilateral process mandated by Action 53 of the Pact for the Future, which requests the Secretary-General to develop a framework on measures of progress on sustainable development to complement and go beyond GDP, as well as the establishment of an independent high-level expert group on the development of this framework. We also like to thank the co-facilitators for outlining the various follow-up actions corresponding to the thematic areas of the document and to explore synergies with existing meetings. The group is still studying these recommendations closely and will provide our detailed comments in the negotiations. However, preliminarily, we would like to underscore that our follow-up actions should be implementation oriented. We believe that increased dialogue is a good first step in accountability to the FFD4 outcome. However, we should carefully consider issues of duplication, potential resource burdens on developing countries to participate in these new processes, and ensure that these efforts do not amount to mere rhetorical engagements. We also welcome further clarity from the co-facilitators on each of these actions outlined and what they envision to be the outcomes of these processes, particularly in implementing the FFD4. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Madam Ambassador, distinguished co-facilitators. I have the honor to make these remarks on behalf of LDCs. We align our statement with the statement delivered on behalf of G77 and China. We firmly believe that a robust monitoring and follow-up mechanism is highly important to track the progress of the commitments expressed in Seville.
